# Shifting fundaments of European higher education governance: competition, ranking, autonomy and accountability
Tero Erkkilä* and Ossi Piironen
Department of Political and Economic Studies, University of Helsinki, Finland
In the present study we provide an interpretation of a general narrative of transnational governance of higher education. All the elements of the narrative – competition, ranking autonomy and accountability – are visibly present in contemporary higher education policy agenda. We examine these not as separate ideas and practices but as an interlinked whole, bringing an amount of coherence to transnational governance of higher education in Europe. All the elements, as they are currently represented in policy statements by the European higher education establishment, are premised on social atomist ontology and ideology of competition. Consequently, drawing on textual evidence we argue that the recent trend for increasing universities' institutional autonomy and accountability has been justified by reference to competitive logic, which, in turn, has been strengthened by the practice of comparative ranking. The article contributes to diagnosing potential misconceptions that frame the current higher education policy-making in Europe.
## Introduction
'Competition' is, without doubt, one of the most policy-relevant words of the early 2000s in Europe (compare Sum 2009). It now frames conduct at all spheres of life, be they private, cultural, social, political or economic. Most people are (at least unconscious) social atomists, since we often assume that entities are 'separable if distinguishable' (Weissman 2000, 2). Moreover, many believe that a competitive environment is necessarily implied and thus competition cannot be escaped. Some liberalists also believe that competition between separate entities will ultimately benefit all (Porter 1990). Whatever the case may be, maximisation of competitiveness has come to define and justify some of the most important policies and policy reforms in Europe (compare Cerny 1997; Hall and Soskice 2001): all things that want to prosper or survive must compete. We call justification of any concrete policy based on this truism 'competitive logic' – a logical deduction from the ideology of competition.
In this article we argue that much in the present thinking that has framed higher education policy-making in Europe during recent years boils down to the ideology of competition. Building on a conceptual analysis of the European Union (EU) policy discourse (Skinner 1969; Miller and Rose 1990; Bacchi 1999; Palonen 2003), we suggest that there is an extent of ideological coherence in the transnational governance of higher education at least in Europe by showing how some contemporary policy-relevant concepts and practices that have had a significant influence on regional, national and institutional higher education policies in Europe are closely and fundamentally

connected. Drawing on empirical evidence – key samples of European higher education policy discourse – we argue that the recent trend for increasing universities' institutional autonomy and accountability have been justified in reference to competitive logic. This logic, in turn, has been strengthened by the practice of comparative ranking: the trend for increasing universities' institutional autonomy has been justified with reference to competitive logic upheld by the practice of comparative ranking (cf. King 2009).
It can be argued that there is a certain circularity in the argumentation of those who advocate for the European mainstream ideas concerning higher education policies, as follows: (1) concern for European and national competitiveness increases the concern for competitiveness of higher education systems; (2) benchmarkings and rankings are constructed to separate success (US 'autonomous' universities) from failure (European 'over-regulated' universities); (3) strengthened market-oriented institutional autonomy is identified as central for improving European universities' performance; (4) direct public regulation of higher education institutions is replaced by alternative mechanisms of accountability and transparency such as performance management, auditions, accreditations and rankings; and (5) concern for competitiveness (regional, national and institutional) – and thus the ideology of competition – is reinforced by the practice of ranking.
We explore this cycle by analysing each of the concepts and the linked causal beliefs in the key documents by the European Union. We start by examining the ways in which competition, competitive environment and competitiveness are utilised in the policy documents. We show how universities' competitiveness is linked to national and regional competitiveness believed to foster economic goals such as growth, employment and welfare. We go on by examining how global university rankings increase the concern for the perceived loss of competitiveness at all levels. Indeed, after the 2003 publication of the first Shanghai ranking (the Academic Ranking of World Universities, ARWU), the concern for the performance of European universities and the European innovation system as a whole got a significant promotion on the agenda of higher education politics throughout Europe. Consequently, we analyse how the main obstacle for improved competitiveness (excessive governmental regulation), the main remedy (strengthened institutional autonomy) and their causal linkage were constructed and represented. We argue that institutional autonomy in this context was conceptualised in economist and market-oriented terms at the expense of traditional attributes of university autonomy influencing policies and institutional practices. This is significant, since concepts not only reflect institutional changes but propel and orient them (cf. Skinner 1969).
We then show how the calls for deregulation brought the discourse of accountability and transparency on the table. Accountability, however, was not aimed towards science itself or the democratic governments, but, instead, was represented as economic accountability towards society as the whole. Deregulation was thus accompanied with the idea that institutions themselves had to ensure accountability not only to politicians and tax payers but to students (employability), employers (work force), businesses (innovations), private funders and education service customers (cf. Neave 2009). Higher education is now conceptualised as an investment whose financial productivity is the responsibility of university managers.
To ensure accountability, the performance and conduct of universities have to be transparent, which means that a range of new monitoring and evaluation mechanisms – including international benchmarking by university rankings – has to be included
in the governance repertoire, a concrete example being the construction of the European Commission initiated U-Multirank tool. The reflexivity over the university rankings is creating new kinds of power relations, where relative national rankings are driving policies at national and EU levels. However, introducing the new audit culture in higher education is prone to bring negative side effects (Shore 2008) and unintended consequences such as reproduction of the ideology of competition and reduction of academic autonomy.
We conclude with two arguments. Firstly, ideology of competition breeds rankings, while rankings uphold the ideology of competition — as a self-sufficient cycle. Secondly, the contested notion of institutional autonomy is constructed as a pre-requisite for success in the increasingly competitive environment: the more autonomous a university is, the better it fares against its rivals in terms of funding, recruitment and research performance, indicated by the high rankings in the league tables. Ideology of competition, practices of ranking and the contemporary ideal of university autonomy are all derived from common ontological premises. Perceived atomist reality calls for atomist solutions.
### Competition
The modern ideas of competition have two primary sources: scientific authority of economic theory and evolutionary biology. Both have been stretched out from their original domain and have had an enormous impact on our social and political thinking. Hence competition looks to us not only natural but also generally beneficial. While explicitly Darwinist applications have not been trendy social thinking for more than half a century, neoliberalism, building on neoclassical economics, has. Of course, there has always been resistance against attempts to make competition an overarching super-ideology to which possibly contradicting values and doctrines are made subordinate. In Europe the strong social democratic tradition occasionally accompanied by nationalist tendencies was able to delay the strengthening of the ideology of competition until the 1980s. If the idea of competition-induced efficiency first influenced monetary and fiscal policies, it was quickly taken to other domains of public policies in European countries.
In the late 1980s and first part of the 1990s, competition at the supranational level was discussed in the confines of the creation of the European common markets. This objective was first endorsed by the Single European Act in 1987, a policy which was reinforced by the Maastricht Treaty and the creation of the single currency: various trade barriers were to be removed and harmonisation of national regulations affecting competition was to be enacted. The principal task of the Directorate-General for Competition was to create a real competitive environment for European companies. Functioning competition within the European markets was believed to foster efficiency, productivity, economic growth and general welfare. Indeed, construction of competitive internal markets was the dominating Commission-led policy initiative during the 1990s – the enlargement project trailing behind – with the effect of trumping contradicting policies and objectives (Wallace, Wallace, and Pollack 2005, 114–115).
Globally the tendency was much similar: under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) the Uruguay Round (1986–1994) led to an unprecedented reduction of tariffs and agricultural subsidies and greatly extended the domain of the negotiations. In 1995 the World Trade Organization (WTO), whose 'main function is to ensure that
trade flows as smoothly, predictably and freely as possible', was commenced.<sup>3</sup> Everyone was to benefit from the liberalisation of global trade.
At the turn of the millennium the ideologies – or realities – of neoliberalism and globalisation finally met. The more the markets were opened – regionally and globally – the more the provincial concern for one's own economic achievement proliferated in the Western world. Global competition entails huge risks and it was acknowledged that not everyone was going to benefit automatically. This explains why the notion of *competitiveness* emerged in the mainstream vocabulary and political agenda. Moreover, competition was no longer reserved for companies alone: individuals had to start competing for their jobs; nations for investments, workers and affordable loans; public agencies for skilled employees; educational institutions for funding, top researchers and talented students. It became habitual for the governments of the smaller states to assess their national competitiveness. International organisations (the World Economic Forum and the IMD World Competitiveness Center) reinforced the dog-eat-dog impression of the contemporary world order by their competitiveness rankings, which – with the help of constant media attention – emerged from near non-existence to the public consciousness during the 2000s.
In the field of European politics, the concern for regional competitiveness had clearly by-passed the previous projects of enlargement and creation of single markets at the turn of the millennium, when the European Council in Lisbon recognised that the EU 'is confronted with a quantum shift resulting from globalisation and the challenges of a new knowledge-driven economy' and agreed on the strategic goal 'to become the most competitive and dynamic knowledge-based economy in the world' (European Council 2000, 2; cf. High Level Group 2004, 24). This link between knowledge and growth had been made already in the 1997 Commission communication *Towards a Europe of knowledge* (European Commission 1997) and it formed the defining causal idea in the foundation of contemporary higher education policy doctrine in Europe. After the Lisbon meeting, research and development was taken to be vital for 'economic growth, employment and social cohesion'. The Lisbon Agenda called for the establishment of a European Research Area aiming at the integration of European scientific resources and growth of private investments in R&D.
In November 2004 the Kok Report – aiming to give new impetus to the process that was widely considered to be stagnating – was represented to the EU organs. It affirmed the gloomy state of the implementation of the Lisbon Agenda and made propositions for streamlining it. The report was based on the idea of global rivalry: 'International competition is intensifying, and Europe faces a twin challenge from Asia and the US' (High Level Group 2004, 12). Urgency was needed to respond to the challenges. Efforts to complete the internal markets had stalled and Europe was losing ground, especially to the US, in the creation of a true knowledge society: 'Whether in patent applications, numbers of scientific researchers, universities' standing in international rankings, numbers of Nobel prize winners or references to scientific papers, Europe trails the US' (20). The message was that for the sake of economic competitiveness Europe had to accelerate its efforts to compete on research and innovation.
In recent times the European Union's high level competition strategy has been accompanied by supporting processes in the field of education policies. The history of European cooperation on education since World War II, according to Corbett (2012, 39), has been filled with 'effort and initiative, success and failure', and comprised with stable ideas such as democracy and respect for cultural diversity but also changes in sector-specific principles and policy goals. After the ratification of the
Maastricht Treaty (1992) and the Treaty of Amsterdam (1997) that gave the European Commission formal but limited competence on education policies, the links between higher education, research and competition have been strengthened (Corbett 2012, 51). In 1999 the Bologna declaration initiated a voluntary (non-EU) process for creating the European Higher Education Area (EHEA) which has been central in shaping European educational structures into a less divergent direction and towards a more harmonised educational market (Ahola and Mesikämmen 2003; Huisman and van der Wende 2004). If the Bologna process has embedded a diverse set of goals and principles, it seems to have incorporated economist goals from the beginning (Corbett 2012; Zgaga 2012). While the declaration did not explicitly refer to intensifying economic competition between power blocks, it – in order to acquire 'a world-wide degree of attraction equal to our extraordinary cultural and scientific traditions' – aimed, among other things, at increasing the European higher education system's international competitiveness (Nokkala 2012).
The Commission both supported the Bologna initiative as well as used it as an excuse to penetrate more deeply into the policy field that was firmly under the jurisdiction of the member states. In a communication given in 2003 the focus was – unlike previously – on the institutional level, on the universities:
Indeed universities go about their business in an increasingly globalized environment which is constantly changing and is characterized by increasing competition to attract and retain outstanding talent, and by the emergence of new requirements for which they have to cater. Yet European universities generally have less to offer and lower financial resources than their equivalents in the other developed countries, particularly the USA. (European Commission 2003, 3)
The main problem, according to this interpretation, was the inability of the European universities to attract talents which led to decreasing levels of excellence.
To summarise, higher education has become politicised in a new way during the last two decades: it is now seen as an organic part of regional and national growth and survival strategy. The education/research-growth nexus has been clearly expressed in various strategy and policy papers by the EU, serving as a justification for pleas for (and joint declarations promising to) reform national higher education systems (Huisman and van der Wende 2004; Blomqvist 2007; Robertson and Keeling 2008). A similar trend can be traced in policy-making at the level of EU member countries: in Finland, for example, higher education is constructed as a part of the national 'innovation system' that should foster economic growth and welfare (STPC 2003; Prime Minister's Office 2006). Consequently, the logic of competition has crept into the domain of education policies defining not only the field of action on which higher education institutions have to act; it also defines their institutional identities as separate entities whose primary function is to compete for survival. Success on this presumed competition is measured by the amount of funding and prestige, but also, more and more, by ranking in international performance indexes which today are manifold.
### Ranking
The first global university ranking was published in 2003 by Shanghai Jiao Tong University. This 'Shanghai list' was followed by another global ranking produced by the *Times Higher Education Supplement* in 2004. While universities in the Anglo-American context had been ranked already before, this was the first time that the global
landscape of higher education was being mapped and, consequently, constructed. In the European context the global rankings have contributed to the construction of a policy problem of European higher education. The core of this problem is the poor ranking of European universities in the global rankings, as the following quote from 2005 shows:
Two recent surveys emphasising research found that apart from a handful in Britain, there are no European Union universities in the top 20 in the world and relatively few in the top 50. The rapid growth of Asian universities, both public and private, is now also challenging Europe – and the US – in terms of doctoral candidates in science and engineering. (European Commission 2005a, 3)
The rankings are based on the same atomist background philosophy as the ideology of competition: they reproduce a political imaginary where universities are seen as separate 'wholes' in whose nature it is to compete against one another globally for funding, students, researchers, publications and even Nobel prizes. Since the mid-2000s these two have been ideationally linked in the policy work of the European Commission (European Commission 2005b): to fare well in the competition for higher education as manifested by a ranking position, is to enhance economic competitiveness.
The response to the rankings has been twofold: the actors are happy to acknowledge the deficiencies and imbalances of the rankings (Rauhvargers 2011), but nevertheless refer to these in their goal setting. The rankings have a peculiar quality, as they not only define goals for higher education institutions (higher ranking) but also identify the attributes for success. The universities are taking notes on the composition of rankings, in trying to 'raise their game', but on a more general level, the rankings have led to the emulation of certain success models – the so-called 'Harvard here' effect. This has led to the identification and copying of certain institutional practices that are seen as recipes for success. Indeed, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) has served as a model for various university mergers in Europe (for example in Helsinki and Dublin), showing ignorance of the particular institutional history and contextual aspects of the model.
Examining the top-down introduction of the tenure track system in the Helsinki-based Aalto University, Herbert and Tienari (2013) provide a very concrete example of how transfer of policy models from one socio-cultural context to another may lead to unexpected outcomes: the tenure model, which, in the originating US context, was introduced as protection for employees from political pressures and short-termism, has, in the eyes of Aalto university's middle-level academics, come to be seen as an instrument for managerial control, elitism and 'cramping of creativity'. Moreover, what is often totally forgotten in the European debates is the diversity of the US higher education system(s), of which the successful and internationally competitive institutions form a relatively low share (see Cohen and Kisker 2010). For us, it seems implausible to import institutional models to an altogether different context, the European *system* of higher education, and expect them to function as they did in their original surroundings.
Nevertheless, in the European Union the university rankings have created a policy problem as there are only very few European institutions among the top-ranked universities, all coming from the UK. During the French EU presidency race in 2007 the above state of affairs became an issue of concern that the European Commission has since been intent on correcting. One of the measures was to create a European university ranking of global scope that would 'do justice' to European higher education
institutions or take into account the 'diversity' in European higher education (European Commission 2007, 5). This European Commission funded initiative led to a U-Multirank tool, which is not a ranking in a strict sense as there is no aggregate number being produced. Instead, a mapping of certain aspects of higher education is created, allowing users to browse the universities for (preselected) attributes (Kauppi and Erkkilä 2011).
But what began as European concern over the limitations of ranking is now becoming part of a wider exercise in higher education assessment. While initially there was a resistance against the use of rankings in the EU context, the global rankings have since become a tool for assessing the quality of higher education in the context of the Lisbon Strategy (European Commission 2008, 2009). And as the U-Multirank tool was leaving behind its pilot phase in 2011, the European Commission had grown more positive for the use of rankings in higher education. In its Supporting for Jobs and Growth agenda, the European Commission notes that the European universities are standing behind their peers globally. This calls for more 'transparency' regarding their performance, that is rankings:
[T]oo few European higher education institutions are recognised as world class in the current, research oriented global university rankings. For instance, only around 200 of Europe's 4000 higher education institutions are included in the top 500, and only 3 in the top 20, according to the latest Academic Ranking of World Universities. And there has been no real improvement over the past years. There is no single excellence model: Europe needs a wide diversity of higher education institutions, and each must pursue excellence in line with its mission and strategic priorities. With more transparent information about the specific profile and performance of individual institutions, policy-makers will be in a better position to develop effective higher education strategies and institutions will find it easier to build on their strengths. (European Commission 2011, 2–3)
At present, the above imaginaries of competition in higher education resonate with the global rankings on economic competitiveness. This also links to the strong discourse of knowledge economy that makes higher education institutions a seeming part of an innovation system (see above). Hence the universities are assessed with economic criteria and the solutions to the improvement of their ranking tend to be economic. In the European context, this has launched a peculiar discourse on university autonomy that is not a reference to academic freedom of these institutions, but – trying to approximate the 'American model' of university – spells for diversity in the funding base of European universities, mostly publicly funded. Arguably, but with suspect empirical backing (see Nokkala 2012), it is because of the extensive governmental and legal regulations that European universities fail to compete against their US rivals. Increased 'autonomy' of the European higher education institutions has been seen as the remedy for this policy problem.
### Autonomy
The notion of university autonomy found a new momentum from the end of the 1990s onwards. Autonomy is a strong principle cherished by academics in all parts of the world, but today it is vigorously defended also in speeches, strategy papers and reports by national governments, academic associations and international organisations such as the European Union and the OECD. There is a broad consensus within the European field of higher education that academic autonomy is to be strengthened. The main reason for this new-found excitement is in the simple chain of causal ideas stating that institutional autonomy of universities – through improved institutional and scientific performance – leads to success strengthening national competitiveness,
economic growth and welfare. According to Nokkala (2012, 61), autonomy 'is framed as a precondition of competitiveness' even 'in the discourse of the Bologna Process'. Let us begin with a cavalcade of presentations of this argument found in some prominent documents defining European visions of education policies from the past decade:
European higher education institutions accept the challenges of operating in a competitive environment at home, in Europe and in the world, but to do so they need the necessary managerial freedom, light and supportive regulatory frameworks and fair financing, or they will be placed at a disadvantage in cooperation and competition. (European Universities Association 2001, 7)
The over-regulation of university life hinders modernisation and efficiency. Minute *ex ante* control hinders universities capacity to react swiftly to changes in their environment. ... In an open, competitive and moving environment, autonomy is a pre-condition for universities to be able to respond to society's changing needs and to take full account for those responses. (European Commission 2005a, 4 and 7)
In short, European universities are not currently in a position to achieve their potential in a number of important ways. As a result, they are behind in the increased international competition for talented academics and students, and miss out on fast changing research agendas and on generating the critical mass, excellence and flexibility necessary to succeed. These failures are compounded by a combination of excessive public control coupled with insufficient funding. ... Universities will not become innovative and responsive to change unless they are given real autonomy and accountability. (European Commission 2006b, 4–5)
The above argumentation has two evident problems. The first is based on both empirical and methodological reasoning. Empirically, there seems to be no proper evidence for the existence of the suggested causal connection between institutional autonomy and high quality research, let alone national competitiveness. Moreover, and contrary to common beliefs, many successful US comprehensive universities are subject to substantive state-level regulation, and, *vice versa*, many lower-tier community colleges have been affected by recent deregulation and privatisation in various states (cf. Cohen and Kisker 2010). Methodologically, it is unlikely that it is even possible to produce sufficient evidence for or against the claim in its general form: there is no self-evident way of defining or measuring universities' performance or quality as we argued in the previous section. The other problem is based on conceptual reasoning (and has possibly normative implications) and the fact that autonomy can be – and has been – defined and defended in various ways. It is our contention that a very peculiar conceptualisation of autonomy that potentially contradicts more traditional accounts (including the notion of academic freedom) has come to dominate the recent European discussion.
There is strong evidence supporting a view that the dominant European higher education discourse utilises the idea of autonomy for lending support to arguments that advance managerial reforms (Neave 2009; Christensen 2011; Piironen 2013). University autonomy is now discussed primarily in its institutional form, incorporating managerial efficiency instead of collegial deliberation and perceiving obstacles to autonomy as emanating from excessive public regulation of financial and organisational matters, rather than from intolerant public opinion, governmental censure or the commodification of higher education. It is treated as an instrument for efficiency and quality, or as a pre-requisite for survival. Autonomy is increasingly seen as the managerial property of the university leadership, and not as the property of the entire academic community.
The challenges faced by higher education require more flexible governance and funding systems which balance greater autonomy for education institutions with accountability
to all stakeholders. Autonomous institutions can specialise more easily, promoting educational and research performance and fostering diversification within higher education systems. But legal, financial and administrative restrictions continue to limit institutional freedom to define strategies and structures and to differentiate themselves from their competitors. The efficiency of higher education institutions and so the effectiveness of public investment can be enhanced by reducing restrictions: on raising private revenue, on capital investment, on the ownership of infrastructure, on the freedom to recruit staff, on accreditation. Investment in professional management can provide strategic vision and leadership while allowing teachers and researchers the necessary academic freedom to concentrate on their core tasks. (European Commission 2011, 9)
That the dominant understanding of autonomy is based on atomist thinking is hardly surprising. Most of us have been taught to link autonomy with liberal individualism (explicitly) and social atomism (implicitly). Take for example the following quotation from Robert C. Bishop (2007, 87):
The Enlightenment ideal of autonomy sees us casting off custom, tradition and authority so we can be autonomous, self-defining individuals. ... And autonomy looks attractive because it seems to empower individuals, enhancing their freedom, dignity and ability to live their own lives. But the emphasis on autonomy comes at the expense of lasting social ties and obligations – after all, one cannot be autonomous and bound to others at the same time.
University rankings are based on this thinking: they highlight the institutional separateness of universities and geographically bounded entities such as states; they assume, encourage and compel competition between (only) externally related separate entities.
But we are not sure whether this is the only way to read Kant, Humboldt and Mill – the liberal thinkers who brought the notion of autonomy to modern philosophy. Perhaps the notion of autonomy has been robbed in a similar way as the whole tradition of philosophical liberalism has (see Simhony and Weinstein 2001) for it seems to be possible to link autonomy with moral, democratic, social and developmental connotations (see Baum 2000, 136–139; Simhony and Weinstein 2001, 14–20; Capaldi 2004, 253, 281, 287–288; Guyer 2007, 95-103; Roberts 2009, 63-69). University autonomy could very well be understood in less atomist, less managerialist and less neoliberalist terms. Science could flourish in collegially and democratically organised universities; in universities where time for research and publication would be slowed down; where time and energy were not wasted on continuous efforts to apply for funding; where teachers had time and resources to plan and develop their courses; where knowledge would be produced socially and where sharing and cooperation would be taken to be as important as individual and institutional competition. Sadly, however, autonomy stands for shorttermism, parochialism and economism at present (Schmidt and Langberg 2007–2008; c.f. Christensen 2011; Piironen 2013). This is enforced by new accountability measures.
### **Accountability **
The calls for increased autonomy are often complemented with demands for 'accountability', as a way of *a posteriori* enforcement of homogeneity and standardisation through mechanisms of assessment and accreditation (Neave 2009).
The concept of accountability is relatively new, and can be linked to the rise of New Public Management reforms starting in the early 1990s in Europe. Before the concepts
in use were responsibility or control, implying more state-centric or democratic understandings of controlling government. As the legal hierarchies of state bureaucracy have been dissolved during the 1990s, the hierarchy-based means for controlling government have been replaced by new forms of economic control. Having previously existed in the realm of accounting, accountability became a concept in vogue to describe the new non-hierarchic means for controlling government. In sum, the above conceptual shift indicates the changes in the perceived mechanisms of accountability that now stress performance (outcome) over responsibility for process (Erkkilä 2007).
The use of numerical information, such as indicators, is also tightly linked to the new demands for performance. As the public organisations are increasingly being made responsible for the performance in economic terms, there is an increasing demand for making their activities calculable. This not only covers the use of finances but has also led to quantification of the actual activities of the organisations that are now being steered with performance management schemes; here the financial information is assessed against various measurements of institutional output. Even universities, largely public institutions in Europe, have not been immune to this development. Moreover, they are in a unique position, because their performance is not only being measured domestically: they also compete in global rankings.
While the idea of accountability through results had been implemented in the universities already before the global rankings, their appearance has certainly heightened such demands. In the policy documents of the European Commission the global university rankings are now coupled with the notion of accountability, and thus, with responsibility that is best attained through institutional autonomy. In a way this seems logical: as the new mechanisms of accountability replace previous hierarchy-based means of control with demands for performance, there is more 'autonomy' allowed for the institutions to attain their performance goals. This often spells the introduction of market type mechanisms in higher education institutions. The new accountability measures therefore complement the diminishing bureaucratic control.
When assessing accountability, three basic components or questions can be helpful in identifying changes at hand: accountable *for what*, *to whom* and *how* (Mulgan 2000). The locus of accountability – *accountable to whom* – has shifted. Instead of being responsible to their academic peers and students, the academic institutions are now assumed to be responsible to the whole society, primarily in an economic sense. In the policy discourse of the European Commission, accountability rose in the early 2000s, in the context of the knowledge economy as a token for efficient management that should be open to professionals coming from outside academia (European Commission 2003, 17). Since the mid-2000s accountability has been identified as one of the drivers of 'modernization'; increased accountability and autonomy are seen to support interdisciplinary and applied research (European Commission 2006a), spelling a shift 'from state control to accountability to society' (European Commission 2005a, 9). European higher education must be modernised for the EU to become a global knowledge economy. Therefore the universities and academics are no longer accountable to their students and peers, but to 'society' at large, which now demands economic performance.
But as accountable to whom is shifting from state control, so are accountable for what and how. Universities' accountability to society is seen to require 'quality assurance' and performance assessments (European Commission 2005a, 7), linked to the Lisbon Strategy of economic growth. These 'new societal needs' demand sufficient autonomy and accountability for improving management, implying also diversity of public and private financial sources (Council of the European Union 2007, 2, 4). The
new institutional autonomy is not about absolute freedom as its proponents are eager to remind us:
Member States should guide the university sector as a whole through a framework of general rules, policy objectives, funding mechanisms and incentives for education, research and innovation activities. In return for being freed from overregulation and micro-management, universities should accept full institutional accountability to society at large for their results. (European Commission 2006b, 11)
Accountability and autonomy are now identified by the European Commission as one of nine measures that would help when facing the challenges set out in the Lisbon agenda (European Commission 2006b). According to the European Commission, university autonomy and accountability have institutional implications as they 'cannot be effectively implemented without adapting governance systems', meaning governance reforms (European Commission 2008, 5). Furthermore, accountability and autonomy make a promise for more flexible governance and funding systems in the forms of managerialisation and privatisation. Altogether, the two concepts have come to signify a group of causal beliefs, now making a full reform agenda. Both concepts are normatively appealing – who would wish to oppose autonomy or accountability? – which allows the political change to be legitimated with their help. In fact the use of these also propels the change, as they communicate the new reform ideas that have cropped up under the commending concepts (Skinner 1969).
This is leading to a circular activity, where global university rankings create a demand for autonomy complemented by accountability, which is assessed against new quality assurance measurements and performance goals, including those set by the global rankings. The above normative ideas of accountability and the related causal beliefs are currently so broadly and uniformly shared by the central actors in the European higher education field that the alternative views of the responsibilities of universities – such as sustaining values common to humanity and academic standards (cf. International Association of Universities 1998; UNESCO 1997) – tend to be drowned out by them. In sum, as the accountability of higher education institutions is now primarily assessed in terms of performance, it becomes a part of the circular logic reinforcing the ideology of competition. Therefore, the rankings not only inform the subject of accountability (for what) but also become the mechanism of accountability (how). This contributes to the steepening political imaginary of competition as the context of European higher education that needs to be reformed accordingly to face the challenge.
## Conclusions
What we have provided in this article is an interpretation of a general narrative of transnational governance of higher education. Our analysis in the European context suggests that there is certain coherence in transnational governance – a view that is often shaded by the habit of looking at particularities, parts assumed separate. All the elements of the narrative – competition, ranking, autonomy and accountability – are visibly present in the contemporary higher education policy agenda; they are connected and based on a common ontological stance (social atomism) that stands as a background premise for a more explicit political worldview surrounding higher education policy-making in Europe. In our narrative this is the ideology of competition – a norm inducing competition at all levels of action.
Looking at the elements together, examining both scholarly accounts and, empirically, statements by key players such as the European Commission, we argued for the following interlinkages: ideology of competition breeds rankings, while rankings uphold the ideology of competition; and a very specific notion of institutional autonomy is constructed as a necessary condition for success in the more and more competitive environment: the more autonomous a university is, the better it fares against its rivals in terms of funding, recruitment and research performance, and the higher it gets on the league tables. Ideology of competition, practices of ranking and the contemporary ideal of university autonomy are all derived from common premises. Consequently, recent higher education reforms all around Europe boil down to competitive logic, but with scarce evidence that the logic will actually hold.
The global university rankings have created a policy concern over European higher education in terms of economic globalisation, not science. This has resulted in heavy referencing in terms such as accountability and autonomy that are normatively appealing. However, references to these concepts render them subjects of political struggle that can bring paradoxical and negative effects for the reforms that are sought. For instance, understanding autonomy in a narrow managerialist sense can lead into circumstances where academic institutions in fact enjoy less academic freedom. Furthermore, the sought flexibility can be hampered by the rigid quality assurance measures and burden of reporting to satisfy the demand for quantifiable information on academic activities. Copying institutional models from one context (or one system) to another may indeed give birth to unintended consequences.
The uncritical references to global university rankings, autonomy and accountability are now paving the way for significant shifts in European higher education. Based on the university rankings, autonomy has been identified as an attribute for success. Nevertheless, in their current narrow understanding, both autonomy and accountability have been leashed to enhance economic performance amid globalisation. Despite the promises of more flexibility and freedom, these concepts are currently part of a global drive for commodifying higher education. The global rankings have a particular role in this, as references to them create a steepening spiral, where rankings both construct the policy problems in higher education and also promise a seeming solution for them.
We contend that our present analysis, together with conceptual and argumentative analyses by others, is not enough to change the dominating higher education discourse or persuade political actors, but it helps to diagnose conceptual and argumentative fallacies and misunderstandings and expose new questions in need of further empirical research.
